You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

" * {@inheritDoc} *

Note: This implementation rescales the * expected array if necessary to ensure that the sum of the * expected and observed counts are equal.

* * @param observed array of observed frequency counts * @param expected array of expected frequency counts * @return chi-square test statistic * @throws IllegalArgumentException if preconditions are not met * or length is less than 2 "

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Failing test: org.apache.commons.math.stat.inference.ChiSquareFactoryTest.testChiSquareLargeTestStatistic() constructs expected and observed frequency arrays whose totals differ significantly:
  - sum(expected) ≈ 42,186,770.79
  - sum(observed) ≈ 29,960,554
  The test asserts the chi-square test statistic equals 114,875.90421929007, which corresponds to the standard computation where expected counts are first rescaled so that their sum matches the observed total.

- Current implementation:
  - org.apache.commons.math.stat.inference.ChiSquareTestImpl.chiSquare(double[], long[]) (lines 64–81) computes
    dev = observed[i] - expected[i];
    sumSq += dev * dev / expected[i];
    without any rescaling of the expected counts. It only checks positivity/non-negativity:
    - isPositive(double[]) (lines 349–356)
    - isNonNegative(long[]) (lines 366–373)
  - The Javadoc for chiSquare(double[], long[]) explicitly states: “This implementation rescales the expected array if necessary to ensure that the sum of the expected and observed counts are equal.” But the code does not implement this rescaling.

- Why the bug occurs:
  - The Pearson chi-square statistic for goodness-of-fit assumes that the expected counts are scaled to the same grand total as the observed counts. If totals differ, you must rescale expected: expected'[i] = expected[i] * (sum(observed) / sum(expected)).
  - The current code uses the unscaled expected, effectively introducing a large systematic offset (because sum(expected) ≠ sum(observed)), inflating or otherwise distorting the statistic.
  - In the provided test, the totals are not equal, so the method’s unscaled computation diverges from the correct value. The test’s expected statistic (114,875.90421929007) reflects the correctly rescaled computation; the implementation returns a different value, causing the assertion to fail.

- Impacted methods:
  - chiSquare(double[], long[]) is directly incorrect per its own Javadoc and statistical definition.
  - chiSquareTest(double[], long[]) delegates to chiSquare(...) and therefore also produces incorrect p-values when totals differ.

Root cause: Missing rescaling of expected counts to match the observed total in ChiSquareTestImpl.chiSquare(double[], long[]), despite the Javadoc promising this behavior.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
